sense: pass on to someone or something else

terms.gloss: refer (a person or a matter) to someone or something else
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; ad and the accusative
evidence: Cic. Att. 9.13.8: ad ipsam tē epistulam rejiciō
Cic. Fam. 13.26.3: sī eōs … Rōmam rejēceris
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to refer to, make over to, remand to”; of an official, to pass a matter on to another authority (rem ad senātum rejicere, often in Livy).

terms.gloss: refer (a question) to someone for a decision
terms.grammar: verb, irregular; ad and the accusative
evidence: Cic. Div. 1.122: ad Apollinem cēnseō referundum
terms.comment: The consul’s word for laying a matter before the senate (ad senātum referre, Lewis & Short). Not “refer to” in the sense of mentioning (see mention) or meaning (see mean).

terms.gloss: refer (someone to a book or a person); hand over (a task)
evidence: Nep. Cato 3.5 (Lewis & Short): studiōsōs Catōnis ad illud volūmen dēlēgāmus
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “good prose; not in Caes.; perh. not in Cic.”.

phrases.latin: sed nē bis eadem legās, ad ipsam tē epistulam rejiciō
phrases.english: but so that you don’t read the same thing twice, I refer you to the letter itself

phrases.latin: dē rēbus et obscūrīs et incertīs ad Apollinem cēnseō referundum, ad quem etiam Athēniēnsēs pūblicē dē majōribus rēbus semper rettulērunt
phrases.english: on things both obscure and uncertain I think one should refer to Apollo, to whom the Athenians too always referred their greater questions as a city

sources: Lewis & Short: reicio · Lewis & Short: refero · Lewis & Short: delego
